Divine Providence over All Created Things

Trithemius argues against those who restrict divine providence to incorruptible or human things, insisting from Boethius, Scripture, Lactantius, and Anselm that God governs all creatures great and small.

The Eighth Question

[Unclear] rules the rest, while truly knowing nothing at all of all other things and neglecting them. But such people have shamefully erred, because the Almighty has providence and care not only for all universal and incorruptible things, but also for particular and corruptible things.^1 Hence Saint Boethius again says:^2

“The high Creator sits upon the earth and, governing all things, bends the reins: king and lord, source and origin, law and wise arbiter of what is just. This is the continuous love by which all things seek to be held fast by the end of the good; for they cannot otherwise endure unless, by a love turned back again, they flow back to the causes which he himself gave.”^3

Others, however, unable to endure the thought that they themselves were being neglected, removed man from the number of corruptible things because of the preeminence of his intellect. They said that God has care and providence for man, but despises all the remaining earthly things. Against their false opinion I judge that enough has already been said, and that to bring forward many further arguments would be wholly superfluous. For Scripture says: “You will save men and beasts, O Lord.”^4 And in another place a certain wise man said: “The Lord made both small and great, and he has care alike for all.”^5

Therefore divine majesty, by its providence, orders, rules, disposes, and cares for all inferior things, both collectively and singly, great and small, corruptible and incorruptible. Its most powerful will brought all things forth from nothing; and again sacred Scripture bears witness: “But your providence, Father, governs all things from the beginning.”^6

Let those rigid men blush, corrupted in mind, impious and reprobate concerning the Christian faith: swollen with empty talk, they take away the providence of him who knows all things, and do not attend to how great an injury they do to God. For what, to use the judgment of Firmianus, is so worthy of almighty God, and so proper to him, as providence?^7 But if he foresaw nothing, if he neglected inferior things, if he did not care for mortal things, then he would already have lost all dignity. Yet it is impossible, as Saint Anselm attests, that God should lose his honor.^8 As the Peripatetic says, among eternal things there is no evil, no corruption, and no sin.^9 Whoever therefore removes providence removes the whole substance of God; and what does he say except that God does not exist?

But let those who deny that God’s providence cares for inferior things tell me now: if God neglected inferior things, let them consider what necessarily follows. If God knowingly neglects and despises us, then henceforth there is no reason for us either to pursue him with worship or to venerate him with religion, since from him we receive no benefit. Rather, neglected and despised, we should neglect him in turn. But if he unknowingly despises and neglects us, then there is no reason at all for us to worship a God who does not know us and for that reason cannot confer anything good, or to call upon him with prayers. For if God does not care for human things, whether knowingly or unknowingly, every cause of piety ceases, since there is no hope of salvation.

What consideration of piety can exist among mortals, what hope for the salvation of souls, if God does not care for human affairs? Indeed, if providence is taken away, whom do we worship? whom do we adore? If there is no providence for mortals with God, then certainly he neither bestows benefits on human beings nor imposes punishments on deserters. He neither can save mortals, nor wills to do so, nor cares at all, nor notices what we do, nor hears anyone’s prayers or supplications. Why, then, do we offer him any worship? Why honor? Why prayers? Or why do we fear and dread so greatly a God who does not know us, who, since we are neglected and despised, can do us neither good nor harm?

Once providence has been removed, neither holiness nor religion will remain. When these have been extinguished, the greatest disturbance of life and a dreadful confusion will follow. With piety toward God taken away, what will the commonwealth be except everlasting confusion? Public trust among human beings will necessarily perish, and the society of the human race, and all justice together, will vanish and perish.

^1. The distinction between incorruptible and corruptible things is Aristotelian-scholastic: heavenly and eternal realities were often classed as incorruptible, while sublunary, bodily things were corruptible. Trithemius rejects any view that restricts providence to the former. ^2. Boethius, the late antique Christian philosopher, is cited here from the providential theology of the Consolation of Philosophy, especially its hymnic and philosophical account of God as ruler of the ordered cosmos. ^3. The quotation is transmitted in damaged form, but it is recognizably Boethian in vocabulary: God as conditor, ruler by “reins,” source, law, and the final good toward which created causes return through love. ^4. Psalm 35:7 Vulgate (Psalm 36:6 in many modern numberings): “You save humans and animals, Lord.” Trithemius uses it to prove that divine care extends beyond rational humanity. ^5. Wisdom 6:7 Vulgate: “He made the small and the great, and he has equal care for all.” The “wise man” is the Solomonic speaker of the Wisdom tradition. ^6. Wisdom 14:3 Vulgate, where divine providence governs from the beginning; the citation directly supports Trithemius’s claim that providence orders all lower created things. ^7. “Firmianus” is Lactantius, Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius, whose Divinae institutiones argues against pagan and philosophical denials of providence. ^8. Anselm’s “honor of God” is a central theological category in Cur Deus homo: divine honor cannot be lost or diminished in God himself. Trithemius invokes that principle against the claim that God could lack providential dignity. ^9. “The Peripatetic” denotes Aristotle or the Aristotelian school. The maxim alludes to the Aristotelian view that eternal, supra-lunar realities are free from corruption, though Trithemius redirects the point into a Christian argument about God.

Divine Providence and the Governance of the World

Trithemius argues that denial of divine providence makes Christian faith empty, and he concludes before Emperor Maximilian that God governs all things, great and small, through omnipotent and uncircumscribed wisdom.

[Fragmentary ending:] They were going. What, then, is to be thought about the Christian faith^1 if God does not care for human affairs? What, finally, will anyone judge concerning Jesus Christ,^2 our Lord and the Savior of all, except that the whole matter is an empty tale and a fiction, if there is no providence of God caring for mortal things? Therefore whatever good we do in this life, whatever evil we endure for the love of God, is wholly vain and useless to us if he has no care at all for us.

Let those who deny the providence of God now see and tremble, when they look upon the dreadful end of their opinion: the worst despair of all. Let no one, therefore, trained by the empty talk of secular philosophers,^3 educate himself into contempt for God; let no one take away the providence of the highest and immutable good; let no one corrupt the dignity of the Creator of all. For all who deny divine providence show themselves both unworthy of, and ungrateful for, the benefits of the most merciful Savior.

It must be firmly believed, and in no way doubted, that this whole world, visible and invisible,^4 and all things individually, whether they are in heaven, on earth, or in the sea, are ruled and governed by divine providence, and that absolutely nothing in the entire universe is alien to his care. For crops and all the other things that the earth brings forth, storms as well, and the variations of the weather and changes of the sky, by which all things that the earth produces come by nature to maturity, divine providence supplies and arranges for the human race, both all things together and each thing singly; not only great things, but even the smallest, so much so that not even the thinnest leaf of a tree falls to the earth without the will of almighty God the Father,^5 who created those things, rules them, and cares for them.

Eighth Question

But if anyone thinks that this immense magnitude of the whole universe cannot be ruled and governed by the eternal God, who alone is, he is greatly mistaken, and is shown not to know how great the power of divine might is. Indeed, he who was able to bring the whole world from nothing into being^6 is also able to govern forever, with perfect wisdom, what he made. For he knows all things, understands all things, and can do all things: he alone, being omnipotent, created all things.

We, therefore, believing the holy Gospel,^7 should above all revere divine providence, and should raise our minds upward, with whatever strength we can, away from the things that are perishable and, brought back to ourselves, be united [conjectured: to it], so that we may faithfully understand the majesty of God as present everywhere. Since it is wholly uncircumscribed,^8 it contains all things, fills all things, embraces all things, surpasses all things, and sustains all things. Yet it does not sustain from one side and surpass from another; nor does it fill from one side and embrace from another. Rather, by embracing it fills, and by filling it embraces; by sustaining and surpassing, it sustains all things. Through bodily mass he is nowhere, and through his uncircumscribed substance he is absent from nowhere. He is not perceived by the eyes of flesh, but is seen through faith in purity of heart.^9

O inexplainable power, O incomprehensible mercy, O ineffable wisdom, O uncircumscribed divinity: you are not contained by parts as a body is, not divided by affections as a soul is, not subject to forms as are all other things that have been made by you. You are in all things and above all things, ruling and governing the universe with perfect wisdom.

By these testimonies, most sacred Caesar Maximilian,^10 it has, I think, been sufficiently proved that this whole world is governed by the providence of God. Since he is pure intellect, simple, uncreated, and everlasting, he knows all things, understands all things, and recognizes all things; and since he is omnipotent by nature, he can do all things that are possible, for whom nothing is difficult, nothing impossible. He created such wondrous things by his power, established them in truth, perfected them by reason, sustains them by virtue, and illumines them by goodness. To him be praise, to him honor, to him glory: he who lives and reigns, the glorious and exalted God, forever and ever. Amen.

^1. The argument is framed as a reductio: without divine providence, Christian doctrine loses its basis, since salvation history presupposes God’s active care for human affairs. ^2. “Jesus Christ, our Lord and Savior of all” reflects standard soteriological language; Trithemius’s point is that Christ’s incarnation and redemptive work would be reduced to “fiction” if providence were denied. ^3. “Secular philosophers” here names pagan or non-theological philosophical discourse when it is perceived as undermining Christian doctrine, not philosophy as a discipline in general. ^4. “Visible and invisible” echoes the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed’s confession of God as maker of all things visible and invisible. ^5. The claim that no small creaturely event occurs apart from the Father’s will recalls Matthew 10:29-31 and Luke 12:6-7, where even sparrows and the hairs of the head fall under divine care. ^6. “From nothing into being” is the doctrine of creatio ex nihilo: God’s creation is not the shaping of pre-existent matter but the production of being itself. ^7. “Holy Gospel” refers not to one specific evangelist here but to the evangelical witness as authoritative Christian teaching. ^8. “Uncircumscribed” translates incircumscriptibilis, a scholastic theological term meaning that God is not bounded by place, quantity, or bodily extension. ^9. “Purity of heart” evokes Matthew 5:8, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God,” here joined to the contrast between bodily sight and spiritual faith. ^10. Caesar Maximilian is Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor (r. 1493-1519), to whom Trithemius addresses the proof in courtly-humanist dedicatory style.

Trithemius’s Protestation to Emperor Maximilian

Trithemius closes the eighth question by submitting his answers to imperial and ecclesiastical scrutiny, professing obedience to the Roman Church and revoking in advance anything contrary to Catholic doctrine.

The Eighth Question

The Author’s Protestation to Caesar

These, most unconquered Maximilian Caesar,^1 are the things that seemed to me necessary to say in response to the eight questions requested by Your Majesty.^2 For you wished also to have my judgment on those same questions in writing, making an estimate of me beyond the truth: I am not to be compared in talent with those whose opinion you heard before mine.

Let pardon make me worthy of indulgence if I have said anything less fittingly than I should, since, at the command of Your Highness, while I was placed on a traveller’s road, I dictated as best I could, at intervals, whatever occurred to me as needing an answer. I say, moreover, from my mind and openly declare that I wish to remain until death a sincere confessor of the Christian faith and in union with the most holy Roman Church.^3 Therefore, if in this little night-work of mine,^4 or in other writings, I have said or written anything otherwise than that Church holds, judges, believes, and teaches, then, as a true son of obedience,^5 by the attestation of the present document I denounce it and will that it be regarded simply and forever as revoked.

For this reason, most wise Caesar, I both humbly ask and urgently admonish Your Majesty that, before you cause my responses to come to the knowledge of those for whom they are destined and preserved, you have them [conjectured: approved] by the judgment of many.^6 For it must be attended to with the greatest care that nothing be set before those for whose salvation Your Serenity keeps watch unless it is solid, tested, manifest, and legitimately confirmed by the judgment of many wise men in the Catholic faith.^7

May almighty God, by his providence,^8 direct and guard you always, for the praise of his name, Maximilian, greatest of emperors. From the city of Neumarkt,^9 on the tenth day of the month of July, in the Christian year 1508.^10

Damaged and Repeated Leaves

Pages 130-137: [unclear]

Pages 138-139 repeat, with minor OCR variation, the closing material beginning “before you cause my responses...” and ending fragmentarily at “direct and guard.”

^1. Maximilian Caesar is Maximilian I of Habsburg, elected King of the Romans in 1486 and styled emperor after 1508; Trithemius addresses him here with the humanist-imperial title Caesar. ^2. The “eight questions” are the organizing frame of the Liber Octo Quaestionum, presented as responses to questions requested by the emperor’s majesty. ^3. The profession of union with the Roman Church functions as an orthodox disclaimer, especially important for Trithemius because his writings often touched chronology, angelology, occult learning, and providential history. ^4. Latin lucubratio literally denotes work done by lamplight or at night; here it modestly describes the present written treatise rather than implying merely casual notes. ^5. “Son of obedience” is a conventional monastic and ecclesiastical formula: Trithemius, as Benedictine abbot of Sponheim, places his authorship under doctrinal submission rather than private speculation. ^6. The OCR reads improbari, “to be rejected/disapproved,” but the context strongly calls for approbari, “to be approved,” since the following sentence requires confirmation by many Catholic wise men. The translation therefore marks the reading as conjectural. ^7. “Catholic faith” here identifies the normative doctrinal body against which the emperor should have the responses tested before circulation. ^8. “Providence” is not casual pious language in this work-context: the surrounding questions concern divine governance of history, so the closing prayer aligns imperial rule with God’s providential direction. ^9. Neumarkt is the place named in the colophon as civitas Neometana; the exact early-modern referent should be checked against the edition’s provenance and Trithemius’s itinerary. ^10. The date is 10 July 1508, shortly after Maximilian adopted the imperial title “elected Roman Emperor” in February 1508 without papal coronation in Rome.
